doc.title: Marian McPartland — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Dream band, reading and closing thoughts
title: Choosing a dream band: trumpet, saxophones and bass
summary: For her dream quintet she picks Roy Hargrove, Sonny Rollins, Phil Woods or Jerry Dodgion, and bassists George Mraz or Christian McBride.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Oh, not necessarily. If you had a choice for a dream, let’s say if you were going to put a quintet together, do you have a trumpet? Who’d play trumpet or cornet or flugelhorn or whatever?
Like now?
Yeah, let’s do now.
Oh God. Well . . . you could say . . . oh God . . . what is the . . .
Let me throw some names out there. Jon Faddis. Nick Payton, Wynton Marsalis . . .
Wait a minute.
. . . Wallace Roney.
Roy Hargrove, I think.
O.k. Roy Hargrove, trumpet. What about saxophone? Doesn’t matter alto or tenor.
Well, maybe both.
O.k. Let’s do both then.
Oh, this is so hard. This would be so hard.
Can be a veteran . . . would it be . . .
Maybe Joe Lovano.
O.k.
Or maybe somebody that’s not around any more, like . . .
Let’s say no. Those that are still living right now.
Those that are still around, because of course I’m always thinking of a Sonny Stitt lookalike or Dexter Gordon lookalike.
Oh yeah.
Where are those guys?
So you’re Joe Lovano or Sonny [?Rollins, presumably] or someone like that?
Well, Sonny, of course. Yeah.
What about alto saxophone? Jackie Mac [McLean]? Charles McPherson? Frank Stozier? Phil Woods? Lou Donaldson?
Maybe Phil Woods.
Jerry Dodgion I know is a collaborator. He’s a collaborator of yours.
Jerry Dodgion, yeah. He’s a favorite of mine. He’s a good player. He writes well.
O.k., bass player, real quick.
Maybe . . . I’d be hard put to not have George Mraz, I think.
George Mraz. O.k.
Christian [McBride] is very good.
That’s the truth.
I think he’s a guy that was there at the right time. John Clayton is another guy. Christian, he doesn’t use a mic, does he?
No, he has that big warm, round sound, unamplified.
Yeah, he does. I don’t know. Maybe I’m used to hearing it. I miss it sometimes.
Yeah, I know when I play with other people it has spoiled you, spoiled one.
Yeah, like . . .
